sections.h2: How a Bethlehem Township sale works
sections.html:
A sale in Bethlehem Township goes through an agreement of sale, a township resale inspection that produces a certificate of use and occupancy, settlement and a recorded deed. The township sits entirely in Northampton County, so the county recorder of deeds and assessment office are the same for every parcel. The township office at 4225 Easton Avenue handles the resale paperwork through its Community Development Department.

The neighboring City of Bethlehem is a separate government with separate sale rules. This page covers only the township, even if your mailing address says Bethlehem.

Bethlehem Township is a suburban municipality of 14.43 square miles of land northeast of the city, with an estimated 26,769 people in July 2025, up from 23,730 in 2010 and 25,868 in 2020. Its villages include Brodhead, Butztown, Farmersville, Middletown, Prospect Park and Wagnerville. Students in grades nine to twelve attend Freedom High School inside the township. Buyers reach the Lehigh Valley mainly by US 22, PA 33 and PA 191, and the average commute is 26.1 minutes.

This is a Certificate of Use and Occupancy inspection that the Code Enforcement Officer performs for the resale of residential property and whenever a rental changes tenants. The application is in the township's Forms and Documents list under the Property Resale/Lease Inspection Program.

  • The form asks for the premises address, the reason (residential resale or change of tenant) and the type of building, such as single-family dwelling, townhouse or condo.
  • It records the settlement date and whether the agreement of sale is attached.
  • It names a contact for scheduling: seller, buyer, or the agent or attorney.
  • The owner signs permission for the inspection.

The inspection checks general compliance with the township's property maintenance, building and zoning rules under Ordinance Nos. 6-78 and 06-23. It is not a home inspection, the electrical portion looks only at GFCI protection, and the certificate carries no township liability for the condition of the house. Call the Code Enforcement Officer at (610) 814-6467 with questions.

File the application once you have an agreement of sale and a settlement date, and attach the agreement if you can. Name one person for the inspector to contact so the visit is not delayed by phone tag. Whoever is named, the owner's signed permission has to be on the form.

Walk the house first. Since electrical review is limited to GFCI protection, the cheapest fix before the inspector arrives is to check the outlets near water. Items that fall under property maintenance, building or zoning rules are easier to repair before the visit than after a buyer has read the report.

Zoning permits cover small outdoor projects, while construction permits cover structural, mechanical and interior work. The township says its lists are not all-inclusive, and it enforces the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code and the 2018 International Codes. Call the Permit Department at (610) 814-6435 if you are unsure.

  • Zoning permit only: detached garages and sheds under 1,000 square feet, decks under 30 inches above grade, patios, fences, driveway expansions and retaining walls of 48 inches or less.
  • Construction permit: structural changes, plumbing, electrical, HVAC and replacement water heaters, replacement windows, decks 30 inches or higher, pools, hot tubs, finished basements, living space conversions and patio roofs.

Finished basements and replacement water heaters are on the permit list, and both are common in older houses. If a previous owner did that work, ask the Community Development Department whether the permit was closed out before the resale inspector arrives.

The township's Interactive Mapping System shows parcel number, lot dimensions and zoning for any address. Tax values, sales data and ownership records come from Northampton County, whose public records site is ncpub.org. The land use code on that site is a tax code, not the township's zoning.

Zoning matters at resale because the township sorts every land use into permitted by right, special exception or conditional use. A use that predates the ordinance may be grandfathered as nonconforming, and variances go to the Zoning Hearing Board. Boundary and survey questions go to the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds.

sections.h2: Selling a vacant or foreclosure property
sections.html:
The township requires vacant properties and properties in foreclosure to be registered, and it administers the program through Hera Property Registry. Owners, mortgagees and trustees register online and pay a registration fee.

If you inherited an empty house or fell behind on a mortgage, register it first and then deal with the resale inspection. Most code enforcement actions start with a concern raised by a resident or owner, and the township does not accept anonymous complaints.

Open permits are the usual snag. After a complete building permit application, the township has fifteen business days to respond, and the work needs a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance after final inspections. If past work was done without a permit, ask the Community Development Department how to close it out before you list.

Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value transferred, with seller and buyer jointly liable, and the county recorder of deeds collects it along with any local share. Ask the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on your deed. For assessment appeals and the annual filing date, call the Northampton County Assessment Division, since that office sets the deadline.

1. Sign the agreement of sale and set the settlement date.
  2. Submit the Property Resale/Lease Inspection application with the signed owner permission.
  3. Let the Code Enforcement Officer inspect, and repair anything on the list tied to property maintenance, building or zoning rules.
  4. Close out any open permits with Community Development.
  5. Collect the Certificate of Use and Occupancy for the buyer.
  6. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the transfer tax total, then settle and record the deed.

Keep copies of every permit and inspection record. The next owner, a lender or a title company may ask for them.

You can list with an agent, sell on your own or take a cash offer. Each route still needs the township inspection and a certificate for the buyer. A cash buyer who accepts the house as is will usually still want the certificate in hand at settlement, so schedule the inspection around the closing date you agree on.

faqs.q: Do I need a township inspection to sell in Bethlehem Township?
faqs.a: Yes. The Code Enforcement Officer performs required inspections for the resale of residential property, and the buyer receives a Certificate of Use and Occupancy. Submit the Property Resale/Lease Inspection application once you have an agreement of sale and a settlement date.

faqs.q: Is the Bethlehem Township inspection the same as a home inspection?
faqs.a: No. Its purpose is general compliance with property maintenance, building and zoning rules. Electrical review covers only GFCI items, and the township takes no responsibility for the home's condition.

faqs.q: Does the City of Bethlehem sale inspection apply to my township house?
faqs.a: No. The city's rule covers property inside city limits. A house in Bethlehem Township uses the township's resale program, even though the mailing address says Bethlehem.

faqs.q: Which county records a Bethlehem Township deed?
faqs.a: Northampton County. The Recorder of Deeds there records the deed and collects the Pennsylvania transfer tax with any local share.

faqs.q: What if my Bethlehem Township house is vacant?
faqs.a: Register it. The township runs a vacant and foreclosure property registry through Hera Property Registry, and owners, mortgagees and trustees must register online and pay the fee.
